newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban seek domination despite truce offer.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban seek domination despite truce offer.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban, buoyed by fresh military successes, say they want their rule acknowledged across Afghanistan, despite a new truce offer made on Monday.
Taleban leaders have offered their bloodied opponents in the north an immediate ceasefire provided that they accept the Islamic movement's sway over the whole country.

"We are not against peace, and the opposition should accept the rule of the Islamic State of Afghanistan for there to be any kind of talks or ceasefire," said Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, the head of the Taleban administration in Kabul, on Saturday.
The Taleban's foes should accept that "the restoration of tranquillity be based on Islamic principles", he added.
The black-turbanned Islamic warriors have swept aside their foes north of Kabul over the past two weeks to retake positions they seized soon after capturing the capital on September 27.

Once again they have bottled up former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood in the rugged Panjsher Valley and have chased troops of his ally General Abdul Rashid Dostum up the Salang Pass, the gateway to Dostum's northern strongholds.
Taleban leaders renewed an offer of an immediate ceasefire and a prisoner exchange on Monday, but gave no signal they were ready to share power with the ousted government or other groups.

"We have been keen on the idea of a ceasefire from the very beginning," acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told Reuters. "We want an immediate ceasefire now, with an exchange of prisoners to take place on the first day it is enforced."
He said the anti-Taleban alliance must guarantee not to use any truce to regroup or reinforce their troops.

General Mohammad Payenda, an Islamabad-based aide to Dostum, said he hoped the Taleban's ceasefire offer was serious, adding that the militia would be well advised not to attempt to make further advances into their opponents' territory.
"Once they get over the Salang Pass, it will be very difficult for them because 90 percent of the north's population consists of (ethnic) Uzbeks, Tajiks and Hazaras," he said.
The Taleban are overwhelmingly ethnic Pashtuns from southern Afghanistan, where their support is strongest.
Payenda said more advances by the Taleban would expose them to attack by hostile civilians and stretch their supply lines.
U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl was due to meet Rabbani in Kabul later on Monday after attending talks among Afghan factions in Tehran at the weekend, a U.N. official said.

The participants, including deposed president Burhanuddin Rabbani, ousted premier Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and former president Sibghatullah Mojadedi, called for a ceasefire, the creation of a safe and secure environment in Kabul, and a prisoner exchange.
"The sharing of power by all parties in the structure of the national government is indispensable," a statement said.
The Taleban, who boycotted the talks on the grounds that Iran was not a neutral party, have made clear they do not want to include rival factions in a broad-based government.
Mutaqi said the Taleban administration in Kabul already represented every Afghan province. "Anyone who is not a criminal can take part in the government," he added.
Taleban leaders have often denounced Dostum and Masood as criminals plundering and oppressing the country.

U.N. efforts to bring about a ceasefire and reconcile the warring Afghan parties have so far failed. The Taleban began this month's offensive a day after three days of U.N.-sponsored talks with their opponents ended without result in Islamabad.
The Taleban, who sprang from religious schools for Afghan refugees in Pakistan, are bent on spreading their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law throughout Afghanistan.
Every important decision is referred to their reclusive leader, Mullah Mohammad Omar, who controls the purist movement from his base in the southern city of Kandahar.
Shi'ite Moslem Iran, where the media have blasted the Sunni Moslem Taleban as tools of the United States and Pakistan, still recognises the defeated Rabbani government.

Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati suggested that Washington might have discouraged the Taleban from attending the Tehran talks after U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robin Rafael met a senior Taleban leader in Islamabad last week.
Pakistan and the United States deny supporting the Taleban or any other Afghan faction, saying they back U.N. efforts to promote formation of a broad-based government in Kabul.
